claims.text: HfNbTiVAl10 has an as-reported hierarchical heterogeneous microstructure.
A machine-learning surrogate calibrated with a small set of tensile and fracture tests and microstructural descriptors can predict Young’s modulus for HfNbTiVAl10.
The proposed surrogate can predict the yield strength of HfNbTiVAl10.
The proposed surrogate can predict fracture-related behavior of HfNbTiVAl10.
The proposed surrogate will predict the target properties more rapidly than traditional atomistic or continuum simulations.
The proposed surrogate will predict the target properties more accurately than traditional atomistic or continuum simulations.
A limited number of standardized tensile and fracture tests can extract phase distribution, nanoscale heterogeneity, and grain-boundary characteristics for use as model inputs.
Phase and feature-size distributions, interfacial character, and local chemical heterogeneity mediate the connection between atomic structure and macroscopic mechanical properties.
The initial elastic slope obtained in a tensile test provides Young’s modulus.
The onset of plasticity provides an early-stage response relevant to yield-strength prediction.
Early-stage mechanical responses are correlated with local microstructural arrangements in a way that can be learned by the proposed model.
Embedding learned response–microstructure correlations can replace computationally expensive full-scale simulations for prediction of complex mechanical behavior.
Alignment, deformation measurement, and data analysis can affect the accuracy of tensile-test measurements of Young’s modulus.
Training and testing at relevant temperatures and loading rates will permit measurement of both elastic and fracture behavior.
The surrogate will significantly shorten prediction time.
The surrogate will reduce predictive error relative to established simulation methods.
Large sample-to-sample microstructural variability may cause the surrogate to fail.
Omission of rare local defects or unexpected phase transformations from the training data may cause prediction failure.
The hypothesis is to be rejected if the surrogate’s independent-test error is statistically significantly larger than the error of traditional simulations.
